statement: On April 29, 2026, in Louisiana v. Callais the Supreme Court held that Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is violated only when the evidence supports a strong inference that a state intentionally drew districts to give minority voters less opportunity because of their race.
anchor: On April 29, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court in Louisiana v. Callais significantly narrowed the circumstances under which a racial vote dilution challenge to a redistricting map can be made under Section 2
only when the evidence supports a strong inference that the State intentionally drew its districts to afford minority voters less opportunity because of their race
context: CRS Legal Sidebar LSB11431, 2026-05-14 (nonpartisan summary of a court holding; the opinion is primary law, vote 6-3 per the Brennan Center page). Holding stands in January 2029 unless Congress amends Section 2 or the Court revisits it; CRS lists race-neutral amendments or codifying the modified Gingles framework as options.

statement: CRS expects Callais to change how maps are drawn: existing majority-minority districts drawn to comply with Section 2 may be challenged as racial gerrymanders, and some legislatures were already modifying maps for the 2026 elections.
anchor: Existing majority-minority districts that were designed to comport with Section 2 might be challenged as unconstitutional racial gerrymanders in view of Callais
some state legislatures are considering or have already enacted modifications to their redistricting maps that eliminate majority-minority districts for the upcoming 2026 congressional elections
context: CRS, 2026-05-14. The sidebar's dissent summary (Justice Kagan) says plaintiffs must now prove a race-based motive, 'nearly impossible'; the majority says the update reflects social change since 1986. Contested: the Brennan Center says the ruling will make Section 2 cases 'much harder' to win; the Manhattan Institute argued before the decision that the problem lay in the Gingles framework, not the statute.

statement: The Brennan Center says Callais made three changes to the Gingles framework that together will make it much harder for voters of color to win Section 2 cases.
anchor: collectively will make it much harder for voters of color to win cases filed under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act
context: Brennan Center (left-leaning), updated after the decision. Agrees with CRS on direction; goes further on effect. The Brennan page also notes nearly half of all Section 2 cases since 1982 challenged at-large local elections, so local effects may be larger than the congressional-map focus suggests (not independently checked).
locator: Brennan Center page, text beginning 'On April 29, 2026'

statement: The Manhattan Institute argued, before the decision, that the problem in Callais lay with the Gingles framework rather than with the Voting Rights Act, which expressly disavows proportional representation.
anchor: The problem lies not with the statute but with Thornburg v. Gingles
context: Manhattan Institute (right-leaning), written 2025-10-24 before the ruling; included as the contesting view. It says the 1982 amendment disavows any right to proportional representation. The majority in Callais adopted a similar reading of Gingles.

statement: The Supreme Court's 2013 decision in Shelby County v. Holder invalidated the Voting Rights Act coverage formula, which rendered preclearance inoperable, while the nationwide Section 2 ban on race-based voting rules remains.
anchor: The Supreme Court's 2013 Shelby County v. Holder decision invalidated the coverage formula, thus rendering preclearance inoperable.
Section 2 of the act contains a nationwide prohibition on voting qualifications based on race, color, or language-minority status.
context: CRS R47520, updated 2026-06-03. The formula relied on 1960s and 1970s turnout data and covered mostly Southern states; a new formula would need present-day justification (CRS). Preclearance returns only if Congress enacts a new formula or a court orders 'bail-in'; no such law is enacted as of this report.

statement: On June 30, 2026, in NRSC v. FEC the Supreme Court invalidated the federal statutory limits on coordinated party expenditures.
anchor: On June 30, 2026, in National Republican Senatorial Committee v. Federal Election Commission ( NRSC v. FEC ), the U.S. Supreme Court invalidated federal statutory limits on a type of political party spending known as coordinated party expenditures .
context: CRS IF13270, 2026-07-16. The vote was 6-3 with Justice Kavanaugh writing and Colorado II overruled, per a law-firm alert (Covington, 2026-06) and Al Jazeera; the CRS In Focus gives background only and says legal analysis is beyond its scope. The limits had been set by a formula; for 2026 the House limit in a single-district state was $130,600 and the 2024 presidential limit was about $32.4 million. The Court left party-to-candidate contribution limits ($5,000 per candidate, per election) in place.

statement: CRS says the effects of NRSC v. FEC are still in flux: unlimited coordinated party spending could help parties compete with super PACs, or could raise corruption risks in party fundraising, and the practical effect may be larger in the 2028 cycle and beyond.
anchor: Some observers have argued that unlimited coordinated expenditures could help parties compete with the financial influence of super PACs or other entities making IEs. Others counter that unlimited coordinated expenditures could increase corruption risks in party fundraising.
it is possible that practical implications from the ruling could be more substantial in the 2028 election cycle and beyond.
context: CRS, 2026-07-16, presents both views without choosing. Covington (practitioner view) says party committees will become a much more attractive vehicle for campaign financing; Senate Democrats quoted by Al Jazeera call the decision an invitation for corruption.

context: GAO, nonpartisan, covering FY2024 estimates. GAO added the unemployment insurance system to the list in June 2022 (GAO-23-106696).

about $24 billion from the prior fiscal year

context: GAO analysis of agency-reported data on PaymentAccuracy.gov (OMB). Agency method: an improper payment includes overpayments, underpayments, payments of unknown propriety (lacking documentation) and technically improper payments, so it is not a measure of fraud or loss. Treasury OIG and TIGTA review parts (SRC-0418, SRC-3682).

statement: In tax year 2021 eligible taxpayers participated in the EITC at a rate of 78 percent, with a dollar participation rate of 81 percent.

at a rate of 78 percent in tax year 2021.

statement: USDA estimates SNAP served 88 percent of all eligible individuals in FY2022, the highest in the nearly 50-year history of the estimate.
anchor: SNAP served 88 percent of all eligible individuals in FY 22, which is the highest in the nearly 50-year history of estimating SNAP participation rates.
context: USDA FNS, report posted in 2025. FY2022 was inside the pandemic public health emergency (emergency allotments, relaxed recertification), so it is a high point and not a steady-state rate; FY2020 covers only five pre-pandemic months. Check for a later-year report.

statement: In a randomized trial with 30,000 elderly people likely eligible for SNAP, 6% of the control group enrolled, against 11% given information and 18% given information plus application help.
anchor: a randomized field experiment in which 30,000 elderly individuals not enrolled in—but likely eligible for—the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP)
Only 6% of the control group enrolls in SNAP over the next nine months, compared to 11% of the Information Only group and 18% of the Information Plus Assistance group.
context: Peer-reviewed in the Quarterly Journal of Economics (Finkelstein and Notowidigdo, 2019). It also finds that those who enrolled because of the interventions had higher net income and were less sick than average enrollees, so lowering frictions reached less needy people first. Population is elderly people in one state, not all eligible households.

statement: Closing SSA field offices led to a persistent 16 percent decline in disability recipients nearby, while applications fell by only 10 percent.
anchor: Closings lead to a persistent 16 percent decline in the number of disability recipients in surrounding areas
Disability applications fall by only 10 percent
context: Peer-reviewed in AEJ: Economic Policy (Deshpande and Li, 2019). The working-paper version reports 13 percent and 11 percent; the published abstract is used. The authors find increased congestion at neighboring offices matters more than travel or information costs.

statement: Herd and Moynihan argue that administrative burdens, meaning learning, compliance and psychological costs, reduce program take-up and fall hardest on the disadvantaged.
anchor: learning costs
compliance costs
psychological costs
administrative burdens often disproportionately affect the disadvantaged
context: Book from the Russell Sage Foundation (2018), a framework built on case studies; it does not itself estimate the size of the effect on take-up. The experimental and quasi-experimental estimates are EV-DEM-119 and EV-DEM-120, which support the direction. The counter-position is that verification and documentation requirements protect program integrity (see improper payment rates in EV-DEM-114), which these studies do not measure; EV-DEM-119 also shows reducing frictions can reach less needy people.

wait times currently stand at 2.4 years and falling

context: DOL core-measure standard (14/21-day first payments). A national result for the latest 12 months was not retrieved from DOL's scorecard pages (still needed); GAO-26-108694 reports a 14.9 percent improper payment rate for unemployment insurance (EV-DEM-114).

statement: GAO estimated that fraud in pandemic unemployment insurance programs was likely between $100 billion and $135 billion, 11 to 15 percent of benefits paid.

context: GAO (September 2023, Biden administration), a statistical estimate; GAO notes DOL said the figure was likely overstated and GAO disagreed. Different method from the Labor Department inspector general, whose estimate is a larger improper (not fraud) total (EV-DEM-126).

locator: Oversight of the UI Program, improper payment discussion

statement: CRS records a government-wide funding gap beginning October 1, 2025 that lasted 42 full days, a second gap of three full days beginning January 31, 2026, and a DHS gap from February 14, 2026 to April 30, 2026 that lasted 75 full days.
anchor: a government-wide funding gap began on October 1. It concluded on November 12, 2025, after lasting 42 full days. A second funding gap affecting activities funded in six regular appropriations bills lasted three full days beginning January 31, 2026. A third funding gap affecting activities funded in the regular appropriations act for the Department of Homeland Security began on February 14, 2026, and concluded on April 30, 2026, after lasting 75 full days.
context: CRS RS20348, nonpartisan. News outlets count the first gap as 43 days (inclusive of both dates); CRS counts full days. The 75-day DHS gap is the longest funding gap since FY1977 on CRS's list. Whether more gaps occur after January 30, 2027 depends on FY2027 appropriations (not yet enacted when this was written).

statement: CRS reports estimates that around 670,000 or more federal employees were furloughed at some point in the 2025 shutdown, and that federal government employment fell by 162,000 in October 2025, largely from deferred-resignation employees leaving payrolls.
anchor: estimates suggest that around 670,000 or more federal employees were furloughed at some point during the shutdown
Federal government employment fell by 162,000 in October and by 6,000 in November
context: CRS R48832 states there is no official furlough count, so 670,000 is an estimate (from agency contingency plans); the 162,000 drop is from BLS employment data and CRS says it was unrelated to the shutdown. CRS also reports CBO's estimate that a six-week shutdown costs about $11 billion of real GDP (less than 1 percent), a temporary effect. Retroactive pay was provided by P.L. 119-37.

statement: ACSI reports that satisfaction with federal government services fell 2.6% to 68.6 in its 2026 study, down from 70.4 in 2025 and the first decline in five years, and that call center satisfaction fell 3% to 63.

Citizen satisfaction with the U.S. federal government is at an ACSI score of 68.6 this year, down from 70.4 in 2025.
The federal call center satisfaction index slides 3% to 63

ACSI's own text says the federal workforce "shed approximately 385,000 employees in the year ending January 2026", which does not match OPM's net change of -258,108 since January 2025 (EV-DEM-082) and should not be used as a headcount. Same finding reported by Government Executive (SRC-2164).

statement: ACSI attributes the 2026 decline in satisfaction with federal services to organizational restructuring and deep staffing reductions.
anchor: those reductions surface throughout the study in weakened customer service, complaint handling, process efficiency, and website scores

The IRS phone data (EV-DEM-095) fits it, while SSA reports improved service over the same period (EV-DEM-103, EV-DEM-104). Government Executive repeats the link without independent evidence (EV-DEM-131).

context: Trade news report of the ACSI release (October 27, 2026); same underlying data as EV-DEM-129, so it is not an independent measurement. It notes only State and GSA scored higher.

statement: Under the reconciliation law the federal share of state SNAP administrative costs falls from 50% to 25% beginning FY2027, so states pay 75%.

context: CRS R48552, nonpartisan, describing enacted law (section 10106 of P.L. 119-21). CRS R42505 confirms the change is now in effect (EV-DEM-142). It will still apply in January 2029 unless Congress changes it.

statement: Beginning in FY2028, states with SNAP payment error rates of 6% to under 8%, 8% to under 10%, and 10% or more must pay 5%, 10% and 15% of SNAP benefit costs.

context: CRS R48552, nonpartisan; enacted law (P.L. 119-21 section 10105). For FY2028 a state may elect its FY2025 or FY2026 error rate; states with very high rates get a delay to FY2029 or FY2030. The national SNAP improper payment rate for FY2025 is 10.9 percent in GAO's table (EV-DEM-114), but the state payment error rate used here is USDA's quality-control measure, so state-by-state rates are still needed.

statement: The Medicaid community engagement requirement in the reconciliation law takes effect December 31, 2026 or sooner at state option, with state exemptions for good-faith effort expiring no later than December 31, 2028.
anchor: The provision is effective beginning December 31, 2026, or sooner at state option.
to expire not later than December 31, 2028

The Rescissions Act was the first successful use of the ICA rescission process since 1992.

statement: BLS reports state government employment of 5525 thousand in January 2025 and 5479 (preliminary) in October 2026.
context: BLS Current Employment Statistics, seasonally adjusted, in thousands; preliminary for the last two months. A slight fall, while the OBBBA shifts SNAP administrative costs to states from FY2027 (EV-DEM-136). Headcount alone does not show eligibility-system capacity.

statement: The Brennan Center estimates that automatic voter registration increased the number of people registered by 9 to 94 percent in the states it studied.
anchor: AVR markedly increases the number of voters being registered — increases in the number of registrants ranging from 9 to 94 percent.
We ran an algorithm to match areas that implemented AVR with demographically similar jurisdictions that did not.
context: Brennan Center for Justice (advocacy think tank that campaigns for AVR), 2019. Matching of AVR jurisdictions to similar non-AVR ones on voter-file data. Measures registrations, not turnout; counts can include duplicate or deadwood records. The Brennan Center published rebuttals to later PPIC/USC and other studies that found smaller effects (links on the same page, not read).

statement: A cross-sectional study of the 2018 election found people in AVR states were one percentage point more likely to vote; another specification found an insignificant association of about half a point overall, with a large positive association for young people only.
figures: one half of one percentage point
anchor: The results show an insignificant relationship between AVR and overall turnout of approximately one half of one percentage point. However, we find substantial heterogeneity by age: AVR has a large positive association with turnout of young individuals but is unrelated or even negatively associated with turnout of older individuals.
individuals in AVR states were one percentage point more likely to vote in 2018 than individuals in non-AVR states, a modest but statistically significant increase.
context: Charlotte Hill, UC Berkeley dissertation (2021), chapter 2, analysis done with Jake Grumbach; Hill was also a youth-voting advocate. Cross-sectional regression on one election, so it is an association, not a causal estimate; the abstract puts the youth figure at 6.3 points. Qualifies the Brennan Center's registration estimate: large registration gains need not mean large turnout gains.

statement: A difference-in-differences study by McGhee and Romero found AVR raised youth registration rates 5.1 points against 2.1 points for all individuals, but synthetic-control estimates by state ranged from +9.4 points in Oregon to -2.6 in Connecticut, none statistically significant.
anchor: Their diff-in-diff model finds a 5.1 percentage-point increase in registration rates for youth (compared to a 2.1 percentage-point increase for all individuals).

ranging from +9.4 percentage points in Oregon to -2.6 percentage points in Connecticut. Ten of twelve states show a positive AVR effect for young people, but no treatment effect rises to traditional levels of statistical significance.
context: Hill's dissertation (2021) summarizing McGhee and Romero (2019), the USC California Civic Engagement Project/PPIC line of work (McGhee is at PPIC, nonpartisan). The original report could not be fetched (pages moved or blocked), so this is a secondary account. These much smaller estimates are what the Brennan Center disputes.

statement: Same-day registration raised turnout of 18-24-year-olds by 3.2 to 7.3 percentage points across difference-in-differences specifications; matching estimates show a 6.3-point effect for 18-24-year-olds, almost the same as for 25-34-year-olds, and smaller effects for older groups.
anchor: same-day registration laws boost youth turnout by 3.2 to 7.3 percentage points
they are largest for the youngest voters, reaching a high of 6.3 percentage points for 18-24-year-olds.
the matching estimates show an effect for 18-24 year-olds that is virtually identical to the effect for 25-34 year-olds.
context: Grumbach and Hill, read in Hill's 2021 dissertation chapter; the peer-reviewed version is in the Journal of Politics (2022, not read). CPS turnout, difference-in-differences with state and decade fixed effects, weighted fixed effects and matching. Self-reported turnout. The headline says youth effects are largest; its own matching table shows the 18-24 and 25-34 effects are about equal.

statement: Preregistration, which lets young people register before they are eligible to vote, raised youth turnout: 13% in a difference-in-differences model, with a 2% lower bound in a lag model, and about 8 percentage points among Florida young people who preregistered.
anchor: From the difference-in-difference model, we find that preregistration laws increased turnout rates by 13%, with the lag model indicating a lower bound of 2%. From the regression discontinuity models, we find that, among those who comply by preregistering, voter turnout is about 8 percentage points higher than a comparable control group.
preregistration is equally effective for Democratic and Republican registrants
context: Holbein and Hillygus (Duke), American Journal of Political Science 2016, peer-reviewed. CPS 2000-2012 and a Florida birth-date regression discontinuity. The body text reports the 13 as percentage points for 18-22-year-olds; the bracket from 2 to 13 is wide. An erratum was issued in 2017 (not read). Ages of preregistration vary by state.

statement: In California, Utah and Washington counties, 1996-2018, universal vote by mail did not affect either party's share of turnout or vote share, and raised turnout by about 2% (estimates 2.1 to 2.2%) of the citizen voting-age population.
anchor: We collect data from 1996 to 2018 on all three US states that implemented universal vote-by-mail in a staggered fashion across counties

We find that 1) universal vote-by-mail does not appear to affect either party’s share of turnout, 2) universal vote-by-mail does not appear to increase either party’s vote share, and 3) universal vote-by-mail modestly increases overall average turnout rates, in line with previous estimates.
VBM causes around a 2% increase (estimates range from 2.1 to 2.2%) in the share of the citizen voting-age population that turns out to vote.
context: Thompson, Wu, Yoder and Hall (Stanford), PNAS June 2020, peer-reviewed; county difference-in-differences. Authors caution it is about normal times, not COVID-era elections, and about universal (all-mail) programs.

statement: Across counties with mandatory vote by mail, turnout rose 1.8 to 2.9 percentage points, and the most precise estimate of the effect on Democratic vote share was 0.7 points with a confidence interval from -0.7 to 2 points, not statistically significant.
anchor: Depending on the specification, the effects range from 1.8 (model 1, P < 0.001) to 2.9 percentage points (model 2, P < 0.001).

Our most precise estimates (model 3) suggest that VBM increases Democratic vote shares by 0.7 percentage points; however, the 95% confidence interval extends from −0.7 percentage points to 2 percentage points.
context: Barber (BYU) and Holbein (Virginia), Science Advances August 2020, peer-reviewed; a different team from the PNAS study. Covers mandatory VBM counties 1992-2018. Holbein also co-wrote the preregistration study (EV-DEM-149).

statement: An Obama-campaign data analyst's studies of all-mail elections found very slight partisan advantages: Republicans gained slightly in Colorado in 2014 and Democrats slightly in Utah counties in 2016, with turnout rising most among low-propensity voters.
anchor: found in deeply reported studies of all-mail elections in Colorado in 2014 and Utah in 2016 that there were very slight partisan advantages in each race.
Two years later, in Utah, Democrats gained an equally slight advantage in counties that had switched to all-mail voting.
The Colorado study found that Republicans outperformed their predicted turnout in 2014 by a slightly higher margin than did Democrats.
context: New York Times report (April 2020) on Amelia Showalter, former data analytics director of the Obama 2012 campaign; her studies are not peer-reviewed and were not read. Small effects in opposite directions, consistent with no systematic partisan tilt.

statement: The opposing view in public debate is assertion, not a study: President Trump said that with all-mail voting no Republican would be elected again, while a Republican data consultant argued all-mail elections could favor conservatives.
anchor: President Donald Trump said that if the United States switched to all-mail voting, “you’d never have a Republican elected in this country again.”
said Republican data and voter contact programs were superior to what Democrats had, meaning all-mail elections could be advantageous for conservatives.
context: Quoted claims in a New York Times report; no method behind either. Recorded so the contested partisan question shows both sides; the peer-reviewed estimates (EV-DEM-150, EV-DEM-151) find no significant effect.

statement: Strict voter ID laws had no negative effect on registration or turnout, 2008–2018: point estimates of -0.1 percentage point for both, +1.4 points for non-white turnout relative to white, while campaign contact of non-white voters rose 4.7 points; the laws had no effect on fraud.
anchor: Using a difference-in-differences design on a 1.6-billion-observations panel dataset, 2008–2018, we find that the laws have no negative effect on registration or turnout, overall or for any group defined by race, gender, age, or party affiliation.
we obtain point estimates of -0.1 percentage point for effects both on overall registration and turnout
+1.4pp for the effect on the turnout of non-white voters relative to whites
the likelihood that non-white voters were contacted by a campaign increases by 4.7 percentage points
strict ID requirements have no effect on fraud – actual or perceived.
context: Cantoni (Bologna) and Pons (Harvard Business School), Quarterly Journal of Economics 2021; anchors from the May 2021 NBER revision, panel 2008–2018. Catalist voter-file data. The 95% intervals (turnout -3.0 to 2.8 points) cannot exclude modest effects; the authors suggest party mobilization may have offset effects on minorities. Contested by GAO's two-state study.

statement: GAO estimated that after new ID requirements, 2012 turnout among eligible and registered voters fell 1.9 to 2.2 percentage points more in Kansas and 2.2 to 3.2 points more in Tennessee than in comparison states, an estimate limited to those states and that election.
anchor: turnout among eligible and registered voters declined more in Kansas and Tennessee than it declined in comparison states
by an estimated 1.9 to 2.2 percentage points more in Kansas and 2.2 to 3.2 percentage points more in Tennessee
GAO's estimates are limited to turnout in the 2012 general election in Kansas and Tennessee
context: U.S. GAO (legislative branch), September 2014, reissued February 2015; difference-in-differences against Alabama, Arkansas, Delaware and Maine using Catalist data. The Kansas and Tennessee secretaries of state disputed it (EV-DEM-156). Quoted from the highlights page through WebFetch; the full report could not be downloaded.

statement: The Heritage Foundation argued GAO's Kansas finding was flawed: Kansas had no Senate race in 2012 while comparison state Maine did, and Kansas turnout of the voting-eligible population was 58.3 percent in 2012 against 56.7 percent in 2000.
anchor: There is no evidence that the turnout of Kansas voters was suppressed or affected in a negative way by the state’s voter ID requirement.
the turnout of the Voting-Eligible Population (VEP) in 2000 was 56.7 percent in Kansas.
the VEP turnout was 58.3 percent
Maine had a U.S. Senate race in 2012 when Kansas did not.
context: Hans von Spakovsky, Heritage Foundation Issue Brief 4380 (April 2015); conservative think tank that supports voter ID. Compares raw turnout across years without a control group, a weaker design than GAO's; also argues Catalist data are partisan.

statement: Preclearance under the Voting Rights Act's 1975 revision increased long-run voter turnout by 4-8 percentage points through lasting gains in minority participation; Democratic support dropped sharply in covered areas, which the author attributes to white backlash.
anchor: Utilizing difference-in-differences to examine the act's 1975 revision, I provide the first estimates of the effects of "preclearance" oversight. I find that preclearance increased long-run voter turnout by 4-8 percentage points, due to lasting gains in minority participation.
Surprisingly, Democratic support dropped sharply in areas subject to oversight.
context: Desmond Ang (Harvard Kennedy School), AEJ: Applied Economics 2019, peer-reviewed; county difference-in-differences. Abstract only read. Preclearance has been inoperable since Shelby County (EV-DEM-011).

statement: In the 2016 election, residents of entirely-black neighborhoods waited 29% longer to vote than residents of entirely-white neighborhoods and were 74% more likely to spend more than 30 minutes at their polling place.
anchor: we quantify a racial disparity in voting wait times across a nationwide sample of polling places during the 2016 U.S. presidential election.
Relative to entirely-white neighborhoods, residents of entirely-black neighborhoods waited 29% longer to vote and were 74% more likely to spend more than 30 minutes at their polling place.
This disparity holds when comparing predominantly white and black polling places within the same states and counties
context: Chen (UCLA), Haggag, Pope and Rohla; arXiv v2 (October 2020), also NBER WP 26487, later in the Review of Economics and Statistics. Smartphone geolocation measures time at polling places, a proxy for waiting. Descriptive disparity; the paper discusses mechanisms but this is not a policy evaluation.

statement: The Sentencing Project estimates 4 million people were disenfranchised by a felony conviction in 2024, 1.7% of the voting eligible population, down 31% since 2016 as states restored rights and correctional populations fell; one in 22 African Americans of voting age is disenfranchised.
anchor: An estimated 4 million people are disenfranchised due to a felony conviction, a figure that has declined by 31% since 2016, as more states enacted policies to curtail this practice and state prison, probation, and parole populations declined.
One out of 59 adult citizens – 1.7% of the total U.S. voting eligible population – is disenfranchised
One in 22 African Americans of voting age is disenfranchised
context: The Sentencing Project (advocates ending felony disenfranchisement), October 2024. Estimates from correctional counts and life tables with recidivism and mortality assumptions. The report says part of the decline is due to a method change. No 2026 edition found.

statement: About 72% of people disenfranchised by a felony conviction live in their communities; 40% have fully completed their sentences and about 29% are in prison or jail.
anchor: Approximately 72% of the disenfranchised population are living in their communities, either while supervised on felony probation or parole or after having fully completed their sentences. The largest share of the disenfranchised population (40%) has fully completed their sentence. People currently in prison and jail now represent about 29% of those disenfranchised.
context: Same report and method as EV-DEM-159 (advocacy organization; modeled estimates).

statement: In a randomized Connecticut experiment with 6,280 people previously incarcerated on a felony, an official mailing on their eligibility raised registration by 1.8 percentage points (from 5.9 percent) and voting from 3.0 to 3.9 percent in November 2012.
anchor: Sample: 6,280 individuals previously incarcerated on a felony
registrations rose by 1.8 percentage points, a 30 percent increase from the 5.9 percent of the comparison group who registered.
increased 30 percent, from 3.0 percent in the comparison group to 3.9 percent in the treatment group.
and actual voting for the November 2012 election.
context: Randomized trial (Gerber, Huber, Meredith, Biggers, Hendry) with the Connecticut Secretary of State, summarized by J-PAL; published in AJPS 2015 (not read). Shows that many people whose rights are already restored do not know it; effects were larger among those who had voted before incarceration.

statement: In 42 jurisdictions with large noncitizen populations, officials who tabulated 23.5 million votes in 2016 referred an estimated 30 incidents of suspected noncitizen voting, 0.0001 percent of votes; forty of the 42 reported none.
anchor: Across 42 jurisdictions, election officials who oversaw the tabulation of 23.5 million votes in the 2016 general election referred only an estimated 30 incidents of suspected noncitizen voting for further investigation or prosecution. In other words, improper noncitizen votes accounted for 0.0001 percent of the 2016 votes in those jurisdictions.
Forty of the jurisdictions — all but two of the 42 we studied — reported no known incidents of noncitizen voting in 2016.
context: Brennan Center (advocacy think tank opposing proof-of-citizenship rules), May 2017; interviews with 44 administrators. Counts referrals and suspicions known to officials, not a records audit, so undetected cases are outside it.

statement: Georgia's 2024 citizenship audit found 20 noncitizens among the 8.2 million people registered; nine had voted in earlier elections, and 156 more cases needed further investigation.
anchor: a check of voter rolls found that 20 of the 8.2 million people registered to vote in the state are not U.S. citizens.
nine of the 20 had voted in previous elections and the other 11 had no record of voting.
there are 156 people whose citizenship status requires additional investigation
context: Associated Press report of Georgia's Republican Secretary of State; the 20 were found partly through jury-duty affidavits. Official release not read.

statement: Utah's review of 2,069,640 voter records confirmed 27 noncitizens, of whom 13 had voted; 25 more were probable noncitizens and 5,007 could not be confirmed either way, and 99.72% were verified citizens.
anchor: In total, our office reviewed 2,069,640 voter records.
my office confirmed that 99.72% of Utah’s registered voters are verifiably U.S. citizens.
During the review, we found 27 confirmed noncitizens
Additionally, there are 5,007 registrants whose citizenship status we were unable
My office also identified 25 registered voters who are probable noncitizens.
Confirmed Noncitizens (27)
Voted Yes 13 No 14
context: Utah Lieutenant Governor (Republican), final report May 27, 2026. The office warns that SAVE and driver-license data are reliable for confirming citizenship but not for showing non-citizenship, so the 5,007 are not presumed noncitizens.
locator: Cover letter, p. 1; "Confirmed Noncitizens (27)" table, p. 9 (the last quotation reads the table's Voted column across its cells)

statement: Heritage's election-law lead testified in 2024 that noncitizens are registering and voting but that the extent is unknown because most states do not verify the citizenship of registered voters.
anchor: We know that aliens are registering and actually voting, although we do not know the extent of the problem since the vast majority of states are not verifying the citizenship of registered voters
context: Hans von Spakovsky (Heritage Foundation, conservative; also a Public Interest Legal Foundation board member), testimony to the House Administration Committee, May 16, 2024. Cites cases in the Heritage Election Fraud Database (not readable: Heritage blocks automated access) and a contested 2014 survey estimate. The audits show some noncitizens did vote, in very small numbers.

statement: States reported an average cost of $249,000 to build online voter registration, up from $240,000 in Pew's 2014 survey, and earlier reported spending $0.50 to $2.34 less per electronic transaction than per paper form; California saved almost $2 million in 2012.
anchor: In Pew’s 2014 survey, states cited an average cost of $240,000 to build and implement their systems. In this brief, with several more states reporting, the average cost increased by $9,000 to $249,000.
States reported spending between $0.50 and $2.34 less per electronic transaction compared with paper.
In 2012, California saved almost $2 million as a result of implementing online registration
context: The Pew Charitable Trusts (nonpartisan; funded election modernization work), May 2015; state self-reports, not audited. Old figures; no newer national cost survey found.

statement: A University of Pennsylvania study of the 2024 Pennsylvania election found mail voters were 25 percentage points more likely to have their vote counted if told of a disqualifying error before Election Day, and 10 points more likely if they could correct it before Election Day; about 20% of mail ballot requestors gave no email address for notice.
anchor: voters were 25 percentage points more likely to have their vote counted if they were told of a disqualifying error before Election Day, and 10 points more likely to have their vote counted if they had an opportunity to correct that error before Election Day, rather than just on Election Day.
roughly 20% of mail ballot requestors didn’t provide an email address.
a new study of the 2024 election in Pennsylvania has found.
context: Votebeat (nonprofit election news) report, June 2026, of a University of Pennsylvania study (co-author Michael Morse) using cross-county variation in cure rules; the study itself was not read. Observational across counties.

statement: As at 30 September 2026, 97.8% of eligible Australians were enrolled (18,470,795 people), leaving an estimated 412,971 unenrolled; the AEC's goal is at least 95%.
anchor: Enrolment statistics as at 30 September 2026
The AEC's goal is to ensure at least 95% of eligible Australians are on the electoral roll at all times.
context: Australian Electoral Commission, official quarterly estimate; enrolment and voting are compulsory, and the AEC enrols people directly from government data (federal direct enrolment).
locator: Size of the electoral roll and enrolment rate

statement: Australia's enrolment rate rose from 90.9% in 2010 to a record 98.2% for the 2025 federal election, which the AEC attributes partly to federal direct enrolment introduced in 2012; turnout of enrolled voters was 89.82% in 2022, and youth enrolment was an estimated 92% in 2025.
anchor:
Enrolment rates have increased from election to election since 2010 (90.9%), to a record high
nationally for the 2025 federal election of 98.2%.

This includes the 2012 introduction and daily maintenance of the AEC’s federal direct
enrolment and update program .
For the 2025 federal election it was estimated to be 92%.
context: Australian Electoral Commission. Rates are official; the link to direct enrolment is the agency's own account (no independent evaluation found). Turnout is measured against the roll, so rising enrolment lowers measured turnout.
locator: Overall enrolment rates; Youth enrolment; National voter turnout

statement: Elections Canada's permanent register covered 96.4% of electors in the preliminary lists for the 2019 general election (accuracy 93.3%, currency 89.9%), up from 92.7% coverage in 2015.
anchor: 43rd general election (2019): Coverage: 96.4% Accuracy: 93.3% Currency: 89.9%
42nd general election (2015): Coverage: 92.7% Accuracy: 90.9% Currency: 84.2%
context: Elections Canada, official register quality measures (coverage = share of eligible electors on the lists). The 2025 figures are in the 45th general election report, which could not be downloaded; a committee witness said all three measures fell in a later election (not verified).
locator: Chart long description (anchors join the listed lines)

statement: Since 2018 the EAC has distributed over $1 billion in HAVA Election Security Grants; by August 2024 states had spent over $638 million (about 63%), about $343 million of it on voting equipment and cybersecurity. The EAC's review rests on interviews and an inventory, not on measured outcomes.
anchor: Since 2018, the EAC has distributed over $1 billion in congressionally appropriated Election Security Grants
States reported spending over $638 million (approximately 63%) of the more than $1 billion in appropriated Election Security funds.
States have spent approximately $343 million (about 56% of the Election Security funds that have been spent) on voting equipment and cybersecurity
Election officials interviewed for the report agreed that federal Election Security Grants help ensure they have the resources they need
context: U.S. Election Assistance Commission, published December 23, 2025 (second Trump administration, before the commissioners were removed in July 2026). Spending figures are state-reported data; the "impact" findings are officials' views, so no outcome evaluation of HAVA grants was found.

statement: In Brazil's largest cities over 20 years, participatory budgeting programs were strongly associated with more health spending, more civil society organizations and lower infant mortality, and the link strengthened the longer programs lasted.
anchor: Drawing from an original database of Brazil's largest cities over the last 20 years, we assess whether adopting PB programs influences several indicators of well-being inputs, processes, and outcomes.

We find PB programs are strongly associated with increases in health care spending, increases in civil society organizations, and decreases in infant mortality rates. This connection strengthens dramatically as PB programs remain in place over longer time frames.
context: Touchton and Wampler, Comparative Political Studies 2014, peer-reviewed; observational panel ("associated"). The link was stronger under Workers' Party mayors, so adoption is not random. Wampler is a long-time PB scholar.

statement: Brazilian municipalities using participatory budgeting in 1990-2004 spent a larger share on sanitation and health, and this was accompanied by lower infant mortality.
anchor: This paper investigates whether the use of participatory budgeting in Brazilian municipalities during 1990–2004 affected the pattern of municipal expenditures and had any impact on living conditions.
channeled a larger fraction of their budgets to investments in sanitation and health services. This change is accompanied by a reduction in infant mortality rates.
context: Sonia Goncalves, World Development 2014, peer-reviewed; independent of Touchton and Wampler. Panel estimates with municipal fixed effects (abstract only read).

statement: Taking part in New York City's participatory budgeting raised participants' probability of voting in regular elections by an average of 8.4 percentage points against matched non-PB voters, with larger effects for groups that vote less often.
anchor: Comparing PB voters to similar individuals who were not exposed to PB, we find that engaging with participatory budgeting increased individuals’ probability of voting by an average of 8.4 percentage points.
these effects are greater for those who often have lower probabilities of voting—young people, lower educated and lower income voters, black voters
context: Carlson, Reynolds and Johnson, Political Behavior (online 2021, print 2023), peer-reviewed; coarsened exact matching on voter files. Self-selection into PB is a limit: people who choose to take part may already be more likely to vote. A 2026 dissertation on other North American cities reportedly found no turnout effect (not read).

statement: Ireland's Citizens' Assembly of 99 randomly selected citizens voted 87% that the constitutional abortion provision should not be retained in full, and 57% recommended replacing it with a provision letting parliament legislate.
anchor: 99 ordinary citizens ‘ randomly selected so as to be broadly representative of Irish society ’
article 40.3.3 should not be retained in full ( 87% of members agreed).
57% of members recommended that it should be replaced with a provision authorising the Oireachtas to legislate on matters relating to termination of pregnancy.
context: Electoral Reform Society (UK advocacy group for deliberative reform), May 2018, restating the Assembly's June 2017 final report (not read). The referendum bill followed the repeal-and-replace route.

statement: In the May 2018 referendum that followed, Irish voters approved the Thirty-sixth Amendment by 1,429,981 to 723,632, with 64.13% turnout.
anchor: Votes in favour of the proposal: 1,429,981
Votes against the proposal: 723,632
Percentage Poll: 64.13%
Referendum on the Thirty-sixth Amendment of the Constitution Bill 2018
context: Official result (Electoral Commission of Ireland archive). Yes share is 66.4% of valid votes (project arithmetic, not anchored).

statement: The Electoral Reform Society argues that the Citizens' Assembly helped break years of political deadlock on abortion, and that the referendum bill followed the Assembly's repeal-and-replace recommendation rather than the parliamentary committee's simple repeal.
anchor: But it only took 99 ordinary citizens to help break years of political deadlock and reach a consensus on this highly polarising issue.
The final Referendum Bill , however, accorded with the ‘repeal and replace’ recommendations made by the Assembly.
context: Advocacy group that promotes citizens' assemblies, writing four days after the vote. Causal attribution is interpretive: party positions and public opinion were also moving. The 99 is restated from EV-DEM-175.

statement: Of the 149 proposals of France's Citizens' Convention for Climate, an analysis of the May 2021 climate bill found 18 included as is and 26 not included at all; the 150 members gave the government 3.3 out of 10 for implementation.
anchor: Of the 149 proposals put forward by the Citizens' Climate Convention:
18 were included "as is"
26 were not included at all
a group of 150 citizens selected at random
the members of the Citizens' Climate Convention gave the government a score of 3.3 out of 10 for its implementation of their proposals.
context: Carbone 4 (French climate consultancy), May 17, 2021, on the bill as it stood May 4, 2021 (before the Senate). Counts depend on what is classed "as is"; the government then claimed most proposals were taken up in whole or part (not read).

statement: Counting the climate and resilience bill and executive measures, 10% of the Convention's recommendations were accepted without modification, 37% were modified or watered down and 53% were rejected.
anchor: considering the bill on ‘climate and resilience’ proposed to the Parliament as well as direct executive directives, 10% of the CCC’s recommendations were accepted by the government without modification, 37% were modified or watered down, and 53% were rejected.
context: Dimitri Courant, academic observer of the Convention, Deliberative Democracy Digest (June 2021). A failure-to-avoid case: the President promised to submit proposals "without filters" and did not.

statement: The OECD collected 289 representative deliberative processes (282 in OECD countries) from 1986 to October 2019.
anchor: Drawing on data collected from 289 case studies (282 from OECD countries) from 1986 to October 2019
context: OECD, June 2020; database of processes commissioned by public authorities (selection depends on what was reported to the OECD).

statement: Where implementation data existed (55 cases), public authorities implemented over half of the recommendations in 76% of deliberative processes and all of them in 36%; in 11% none were implemented.
anchor: There was data available for 55 cases

In three quarters (76%) of these cases, the public authorities implemented over half of the recommendations. In four in ten (36%) of these cases, it implemented all of them. Only in six (11%) of these 55 cases were none of the recommendations implemented.
whether there is a general tendency to ‘cherrypick’
context: OECD 2020, Figure 4.9 (13 countries plus EU, 1997-2019). Only 55 of 289 cases had data, likely the better-documented ones; the OECD itself flags possible cherry-picking.

statement: Tracking the same individuals over time, declines in local coverage of House elections between 2010 and 2014 were followed by reductions in citizens' political knowledge and participation; local papers published less, and less substantive, political news.
anchor: Drawing on a content analysis of more than 10,000 stories about US House campaigns in 2010 and 2014, we show that local newspapers over this period published less, and less substantive, political news.
reveals that reductions in citizens’ political knowledge and participation follow declines in coverage about congressional elections.
context: Hayes and Lawless, Journal of Politics 80(1), peer-reviewed; CCES panel linked to content analysis. The body text calls the effects modest.

statement: Medill counted 213 news desert counties in 2025, up from 206, and another 1,524 counties with only one local news source, so about 50 million Americans have limited or no access to local news; newspaper closures were 136 in the past year, against about 150 news desert counties twenty years earlier.
anchor: The number of news desert counties rose to 213 in 2025, a jump from 206 in last year’s report.
In another 1,524 counties, there’s only one remaining news source.
Taken together, some 50 million Americans have limited to no access to local news.
Twenty years ago, there were about 150 news desert counties
The rise in news deserts was accompanied by an increase in newspaper closures, which ticked up to 136 this past year
context: Medill School of Journalism, Northwestern University, State of Local News 2025 (release of October 20, 2025, quoted through WebFetch). The 2026 edition may already be out; check. University research project counting outlets, not an effects study.

statement: State civics exams raise young people's civic knowledge most for those with less exposure at home, specifically Latinos and immigrants: the study finds modest support that graduation-linked exams matter more and strong support for this compensation effect.
anchor: We further hypothesize that civics requirements have the biggest effect on young people with less exposure to information about the U.S. political system at home, specifically Latinos and, especially, immigrants—the compensation hypothesis.

We test these hypotheses with the 2006 and 2010 National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) civics test administered to high school students, and with a large national survey of 18–24 year-olds.
we find modest support for the incentive hypothesis and strong support for the compensation hypothesis.
context: Campbell (Notre Dame) and Niemi (Rochester), APSR 2016, peer-reviewed; cross-state comparisons of knowledge, not turnout.

statement: The civics test graduation requirement adopted by 18 states between 2016 and 2022 did not raise youth turnout: young people in those states were at most 1.5 percentage points more likely to vote, not statistically significant.
anchor: Between 2016 and 2022, 18 states implemented a version of the Civics Education Initiative (CEI), which requires high school students to take or pass a standardized civics test as a condition for graduation.

young people in states requiring the civics tests for graduation were at most 1.5 percentage points more likely to vote than peers in states that didn’t have such civics requirements, which is not statistically significant.
context: Penn State news release on Jung and Gopalan, Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis (2023, peer-reviewed; not read). Difference-in-differences on self-reported CPS turnout. Graded C because only the release was read. Test proponents say turnout was never the aim (not anchored).

statement: Code for America reports that 75% of Medicaid clients with a streamlined (automatic) renewal trusted the agency to often or always do the right thing for people like them, against 66% of those who went through the standard renewal, but assignment was not random.
anchor: We found 75% of clients with the streamlined experience trusted DHS to often or always do the right thing for people like them
in contrast to 66% of clients who had to complete the standard renewal process.
Because it wasn't random who received the more streamlined renewal process,
we can't say for certain that automatic renewals caused clients to have higher trust in their government.

statement: On April 6, 2017 the Senate extended majority cloture to Supreme Court nominations by the same method as in 2013, so cloture on any nomination now needs a majority of those voting; CRS notes such proceedings are called the 'nuclear option' because they were arguably at variance with established Senate procedure.
anchor: On April 6, 2017, the Senate reinterpreted Rule XXII to allow a majority of Senators voting, a quorum being present, to invoke cloture on nominations to the U.S. Supreme Court.

The proceedings of April 6, 2017, were similar to those of November 21, 2013, when the Senate reinterpreted the cloture rule to lower the threshold for invoking cloture for all nominations except to the Supreme Court.
Proceedings of this kind have been called “the nuclear option” because they required actions arguably at variance with established principles underlying Senate procedure.
As a result of these two precedents, the Senate can now invoke cloture on any nomination by a majority vote.
context: CRS. Cloture on legislation still needs three-fifths; cloture counts are in EV-DEM-073.

statement: CRS finds it unresolved whether the National Popular Vote compact needs congressional consent under the Compact Clause, since the test asks whether a compact enhances state power against the federal government; supporters cite states' plenary power over appointing electors (McPherson v. Blacker), while opponents argue the Constitution's structure bars states from turning the Electoral College into a national popular vote.
anchor: Accordingly, the central legal issue with respect to the Compact Clause is whether a given interstate compact requires the consent of Congress.

whether such an arguably hypothetical and de minimis diminishment of federal power through the NPV would be sufficient to require congressional consent under the Compact Clause is simply unresolved by the relevant case law.

Supporters of the NPV argue that the Constitution provides the legal means for states to transform the presidential election system into one where the President is elected based solely on the result of the national popular vote.

Others have argued that the structure of the Constitution and historical evidence suggest that the states do not have such vast discretion in appointing electors as to functionally transform the election for President into a national popular referendum.
context: CRS (2019 version, the latest). It predates Chiafalo v. Washington (2020), which upheld states' power to bind electors and which compact supporters cite; that ruling is not in the register. Membership counts are in EV-DEM-076 (the compact's own organization).
